units.title: Hello, Java
units.summary: Write your first Java program with a class, a main method and System.out.println, and learn how to compile and run it.

lesson.md: Java programs are made of **classes**. A class is a named block of code. Every program needs at least one class; here it is called `Main`. Inside the class, the program starts in a **method** called `main`. Curly braces `{ }` mark where a block begins and where it ends.

The line `public static void main(String[] args)` is the same in every program. For now, copy it as it is. You learn what `public`, `static`, `void` and `String[] args` mean later in this course. `System.out.println` prints the value in the parentheses and then starts a new line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello"`, is a **string**.

Every instruction is called a **statement** and ends with a semicolon `;`. `System.out.print` (without `ln`) prints without starting a new line, so the next output continues on the same line. Java is **case-sensitive**: `System` and `system` are different names, and only `System` works.

You save the code in a file that ends in `.java`. A `public class` must be in a file with the same name, so the class `Main` goes into `Main.java`. The command `javac Main.java` **compiles** the code: it checks it for errors and translates it into a file called `Main.class`. Then `java Main` runs the program. If the code has an error, `javac` reports it and nothing runs.
Since Java 11, the command `java Main.java` compiles and runs a single file in one step. This is handy for small programs like the ones in this course.

Numbers do not need quotes. Java calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` (times) and `/` (divided by). It calculates the result first and then prints it. As in mathematics, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses come first.

When you divide two whole numbers with `/`, Java drops the rest: `7 / 2` is `3`. The operator `%` gives you the rest of a division: `7 % 2` is `1`. Write `7.0 / 2` to get a result with decimals: `3.5`.
`"5"` with quotes is a string, `5` without quotes is a number. For strings, `+` joins the text: `"2" + "3"` gives `23`, but `2 + 3` gives `5`.

card: `public static void main(String[] args) { }` is where it starts
`System.out.println(x);` prints `x` and a new line, `print` does not

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables and meet the types int, double, boolean, char and String, plus var and final.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. In Java, every variable has a **type** that says what kind of value it holds. You write the type, the name, `=` and the value: `int age = 30;`. Here `=` means "store", not "is equal to".

To change a variable, assign a new value without the type: `score = score + 5;` takes the old value, adds `5` and stores the result. `score += 3;` is a short form of `score = score + 3;`. `score++;` adds `1`, and `score--;` subtracts `1`.

`int` holds whole numbers, `double` holds numbers with decimals, and `boolean` holds `true` or `false`. `char` holds one single character in single quotes, like `'A'`. `String` holds text in double quotes. It starts with a capital `S` because it is a class, not a basic type.

Java checks the types when it compiles. A `String` never fits into an `int` variable. An `int` fits into a `double`: `double x = 7;` stores `7.0`. A `double` does not fit into an `int` on its own. You need a **cast**: `(int) 3.9` cuts off the decimals and gives `3`.

With `var`, Java finds the type from the value: `var count = 5;` creates an `int`. The type is still fixed, so `count` can never hold a `String` later. You can use `var` only for variables inside a method that get a value right away.

A variable marked `final` cannot change after it gets its value. If you try, the program does not compile. Names of such constants are often written in capital letters with `_` between the words, like `MAX_SPEED`.
From now on, short code in the exercises often shows only the lines inside `main`, or only the parts inside the class. To run such code, you put it into a full program like the ones above.

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Join strings with +, work with length, charAt, substring and toUpperCase, and compare text with equals.

lesson.md: The operator `+` joins strings. This is called **concatenation**. When one side is a string and the other side is a number, Java turns the number into text first.

Java reads `+` from left to right. `"Sum: " + 2 + 3` first gives `"Sum: 2"` and then `"Sum: 23"`. Use parentheses to calculate first: `"Sum: " + (2 + 3)`. In `2 + 3 + " apples"`, the numbers come first, so Java adds them.

A string has **methods**: actions you call with a dot and parentheses. `word.length()` gives the number of characters. `toUpperCase()` and `toLowerCase()` give a new string in capital or small letters. The original string never changes: strings in Java are **immutable**.

Every character has a position, called its **index**. The index starts at `0`. `charAt(i)` gives the `char` at index `i`. `substring(start, end)` gives the characters from `start` up to, but not including, `end`. `substring(start)` goes to the end of the string.
The last index is `length() - 1`. `"Hello".charAt(5)` stops the program with an error called `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

To check if two strings contain the same text, use `a.equals(b)`. It gives `true` or `false`. Do not use `==` for strings: it checks if both names point to the very same object in memory. Two strings with the same text can be different objects. `equalsIgnoreCase` compares and ignores capital and small letters.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Make decisions with if and else, comparison and logical operators, switch expressions and the ternary operator.

lesson.md: An `if` statement runs a block of code only when a condition is `true`. The condition goes in parentheses `( )`, the code in curly braces `{ }`. After the block, the program continues as normal.

Comparisons give a `boolean`: `==` (equal to), `!=` (not equal to), `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=` (less than or equal to) and `>=` (greater than or equal to). Do not mix up `==` and `=`: `=` stores a value, `==` compares two values.
The block after `else` runs when the condition is `false`. With `else if` you can test more conditions. Java checks them from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is `true`.

**Logical operators** combine conditions. `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are `true`. `||` (or) is `true` when at least one side is `true`. `!` (not) turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.

A `switch` expression picks a value depending on another value. Each `case` lists one or more values, then an arrow `->` and the result. `default` covers all other values. Because the whole `switch` gives a value, a semicolon follows the closing brace.
The **ternary operator** `condition ? a : b` is a short `if` that gives a value: `a` when the condition is `true`, otherwise `b`.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for, while and do-while loops, go through arrays with the enhanced for, and use break and continue.

lesson.md: A `for` loop repeats a block of code. Its header has three parts, separated by semicolons: the start (`int i = 1`), the condition (`i <= 3`) and the update (`i++`). Java runs the block as long as the condition is `true` and does the update after each round.
The update can be anything that changes the variable. `i += 5` counts in steps of five, and `i--` counts down. A variable outside the loop can collect a result, for example a sum.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. It checks the condition before each round. Make sure that something in the block changes the condition, or the loop never ends.
A `do-while` loop runs the block first and checks the condition after it. So the block always runs at least once. Note the semicolon after `while (...)`.

An **array** holds several values of the same type: `String[] names = {"Ana", "Ben"};`. The unit about arrays and lists explains them in detail. The enhanced `for` loop goes through all values: read `for (String name : names)` as "for each `name` in `names`".

lesson.md: `break` ends a loop right away. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one.

units.title: Methods
units.summary: Write your own static methods with parameters and return values, and overload a method for different types.

lesson.md: A **method** is a named block of code that you can run again and again by calling its name. `main` is a method too. You write your own methods inside the class, next to `main`. For now, start each one with `static`. The word `void` means that the method gives no result back.

A method can take **parameters**: values it gets from the caller. You list them in the parentheses, each with a type and a name, separated by commas. When you call the method, you pass the values, called **arguments**, in the same order.

lesson.md: Instead of `void`, you can write the type of a result, for example `int`. Then the method must end with `return` and a value of that type. `return` sends the value back to the caller, which can store it, print it or calculate with it.
`return` ends the method right away. So a method can return early from inside an `if`, and the code after it does not run.
A parameter is a copy of the argument. If a method changes its parameter, the variable of the caller stays the same. Variables you create inside a method exist only in that method.

Several methods can have the same name if their parameters are different: a different number of parameters or different types. This is called **overloading**. Java picks the method whose parameters match the arguments.

units.title: Arrays and lists
units.summary: Store many values in arrays and ArrayLists, read and change them by index, and go through them with loops.

lesson.md: An **array** holds a fixed number of values of the same type. `int[] scores = {90, 75, 82};` creates an array with three `int` values: `[]` after the type means "array of". You read a value by its index in square brackets, starting at `0`: `scores[0]`. You change it with `scores[1] = 80;`.

`scores.length` gives the size of an array, without parentheses. `new int[3]` creates an array with three zeros. To print a whole array, use `Arrays.toString`. It is in the package `java.util`, so the file needs the line `import java.util.Arrays;` before the class.
You can go through an array with a counting `for` loop, from `0` to `length - 1`, or with the enhanced `for` loop. Use the counting loop when you need the index.
The last index is `length - 1`. An index outside the array stops the program with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
Now you can read `String[] args` in `main`: it is an array of strings. It holds the words you type after `java Main` on the command line.

An array cannot grow. An `ArrayList` can. `ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();` creates an empty list of strings: the type of the values goes in angle brackets `< >`, and `new` creates the list. Its methods are `add`, `get`, `set`, `remove`, `size` and `contains`. It needs `import java.util.ArrayList;`.

Lists hold objects, so for numbers you write `Integer` instead of `int` (and `Double` instead of `double`). `List.of(4, 8, 15)` creates a short list in one step. The type `List<Integer>` and `List.of` need `import java.util.List;`. The enhanced `for` loop works with lists too.

A list from `List.of` cannot change. Calling `add` on it stops the program with an `UnsupportedOperationException`. If you need to change it, make an `ArrayList` copy: `new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2))`.

units.title: Classes and records
units.summary: Create your own types with classes, fields, constructors and methods, and hold data in short records.

lesson.md: A class is a plan for your own type. **Fields** are the variables that each object of the class has. You create an **object** with `new`, and you reach its fields with a dot.

Here the class `Dog` is in the same file as `Main`, before it. Only one class in a file can be `public`. In bigger projects, each class has its own file. Fields that you do not set get a default value: `0` for numbers and `false` for `boolean`.

A **constructor** sets up a new object. It has the same name as the class and no return type, and it runs when you call `new`. Inside it, `this` means the object being created: `this.name` is the field, and `name` alone is the parameter.

Methods without `static` belong to an object. You call them on an object with a dot, like `acc.deposit(50)`, and they can read and change the fields of that object. A `static` method belongs to the class itself and needs no object. That is why `main` is `static`.

`public` means that all classes can use something. In real projects, fields are often `private`, like `private double balance;`. Then only the class itself can use them, and other code must call its methods.

A **record** is a short way to write a class that only holds data: `record Point(int x, int y) {}`. Java creates the fields, the constructor and a method for each value, like `p.x()`. A record also prints in a readable form, `equals` compares the values, and the values cannot change.
If you print an object of a normal class, you get something like `Dog@1b6d3586`, the class name and a code. Records print their values instead.

card: `Dog(String name) { this.name = name; }` is a constructor
`Dog d = new Dog("Rex");` creates an object
`d.bark()` calls a method on the object
